newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's GITIC Enterprises still seen strong on debut.
newsitem.headline: HK's GITIC Enterprises still seen strong on debut.

text.p: Shares of GITIC Enterprises Ltd are poised for strong gains on their trading debut on Wednesday, extending the recent flurry of speculative demand for "red chips" backed by an asset-injection concept, analysts said.
A relatively high grey market price above HK$3.00 (40 U.S. cents) and expectations of heavy demand may also bolster the shares despite unresolved questions about the offer, they said.
"I think the stock should gain support at its grey market price," said Henri Lui, an analyst at Mansion House.
GITIC Enterprises imports and sells construction materials in Hong Kong and China, and also owns the second floor of a shopping mall at GITIC Plaza in the southern China boom city of Guangzhou.

The company's much anticipated initial public offering (IPO) of shares is expected to become one of Hong Kong's most popular ever. The company's 100 million new shares, offered at HK$1.05 (14 U.S. cents) each, is seen 900 to 1,000 times subscribed.
That would break the record of carmaker Denway Investment Ltd in February 1993. Its issue of 330 million shares was 657 times oversubscribed.
GITIC Enterprises is due to reveal its subscription results on Monday.
Analysts said GITIC Enterprises has benefited from exposure to China. Other attractions include the relatively small size of the issue and the company's close relationship with its parent.

GITIC Enterprises is indirectly controlled by the Guangdong provincial government's investment arm, Guangdong International Trust and Investment Corp (GITIC), which had total assets of about 20.56 billion yuan ($2.48 billion) at the end of 1995.
Analysts generally expect its parent to inject properties and financial units into the company.
The stock is expected to perform strongly despite market speculation that the offering had encountered problems which could possibly lead to a withdrawal of the listing.

Rumours swirled in the market last Tuesday that GITIC Enterprises may not have obtained all necessary approval for the float from the China Securities Regulation Commission, the mainland's securities watchdog.
On Wednesday, GITIC Enterprises responded by saying that its Hong Kong IPO and listing plan would proceed on schedule. But some brokers said the company did not fully clarify the rumours.

"I see a neutral impact on its IPO response given its strong subscription level," said Patrick Cheng, a director at HSBC Investment Bank, referring to the recent market speculation. "Its debut is expected to be strong."
Analysts said the uncertainty could cool recent speculative fever for so-called "red chips" -- China-related companies often with parents based on the mainland.

Demand for such stocks has been fed by hopes their parents would inject them with high quality assets. But the analysts said it may not be easy for red chips to receive asset injections if regulators cracked down on such moves.

"Worries over the feasibility of (GITIC Enterprises') future asset plans are likely to drive short-term investors away in the short run," Lui said. "But apart from that, the prospects for its construction materials business remains bright."
Analysts said they expected strong demand for construction materials in coming years due to booming property and infrastructure projects in both Hong Kong and China.
